extracted.intended_audience: poets and literary friends (Romantic-era readers and critics); readers of Letters of Charles Lamb
extracted.subtask_short: literary criticism of poetry and epitaphs
extracted.subtask_description: Letters of Charles Lamb giving evaluative guidance on poetry, epitaphs, diction, editing, and presentation — i.e., practical and aesthetic criteria for composing and judging poems and epitaphs. The material is informal, epistolary criticism aimed at a poet (Wordsworth) and other literary acquaintances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphs should 'go to the bottom' / express plain feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: An epitaph should reach 'to the bottom' and render the plain feeling under ornate phrasing; translating a turgid epitaph into plain feeling is 'perfectly a test.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given where a turgid epitaph is translated into plain feeling (Wordsworth's continuation of the 'Essay on Epitaphs' praised as 'the only sensible thing ... and it goes to the bottom'). Use plain, sincere expression rather than rhetorical swellings; test a good epitaph by whether its core feeling remains when pared down into plain language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glib, patent, and platitudinous epitaphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Epitaphs that are 'trim and sprag, and patent' and that display artful but vacuous variety (the Thames Ditton poet who diversified 'strains and his rhymes' so that 'the same thought never occurs twice') are to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't produce inscriptions that are merely verbal cleverness or mechanical variation without thought; avoid writing that treats 'death' as a word to be used glibly rather than as subject of genuine meditation. Aim for authenticity rather than clever novelty for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphs must be suited to the deceased (avoid misplaced commonplaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscriptions must fit the person and circumstance; a misplaced common sentence (e.g., 'Honor thy father and thy mother' appended to an epitaph of an infant) shows failure of judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check appropriateness: a sententia or biblical proverb may be seasonable in one context but absurd or hurtful in another. Tailor sentiments to age, status, and situation of the deceased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poems can (and should) be 'conversational' yet noble
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem may succeed by being a 'noble conversational poem' — accessible in tone like conversation but elevated in feeling and dignity (Lamb on Wordsworth's 'a day in heaven').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for a balance: conversational ease that carries weight. Avoid stiffness or artificial loftiness; aim for natural speech heightened to noble effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and 'aliveness' of lines — avoid empty ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines should be 'alive' and not merely 'fine words' with an 'aching vacuum of matter'; genuine invention and substance are preferable to ornate diction without content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer matter-ful diction (substantive thought and feeling) to elegant but hollow phrasing. Beware of authorship that substitutes sonorous language for real imaginative content (Lamb's critique of Lord Thurlow's 'fine words' but 'an aching vacuum of matter').

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance subject-matter so readers of different backgrounds are not alienated
rubrics_metrics.description: Rural or specialized imagery should not 'overpower and discountenance a poor Londoner' — poetry should not so monopolize one milieu that it excludes readers from other backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using strong local or specialized material, maintain touchpoints accessible to readers beyond that setting. Avoid making the poem so provincial or intense in subject that it alienates those unfamiliar with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evocative sensory detail and transformative description
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective writing renders immediate sensory and transforming experiences (e.g., 'the instantaneous coolness and calming, almost transforming, properties of a country church just entered' are exactly what Wordsworth 'reduced into words').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to capture and convey the precise sensory quality and emotional transformation of an experience. Specific, sensed detail that conveys a change in mood or perception is a mark of strong poetic description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve authentic particulars; avoid falsifying substitutes in editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute artificial or 'shell' elements for genuine household particulars (Lamb objects to a substitution 'whereof leaves it ... less complete' — e.g., replacing a real implement with a 'shell' as a concession).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In revising or preparing texts, favour the authentic concrete detail that supports meaning; resist editorial changes made merely to placate critics if they sacrifice truth or the original character of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and tonal coherence across a poet's work or collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency is a virtue: 'All the rest of your poems are so much of a piece they might have been written in the same week' — coherence across pieces is admired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collections benefit from a recognisable, coherent tone or manner. Distinct pieces may still show variety, but overall unity of sensibility and voice strengthens a body of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid endings that undermine a poem's moral or intent
rubrics_metrics.description: A closing verse that introduces ambiguity or contradiction (the 'last verse of Susan' which 'threw a kind of dubiety upon Susan's moral conduct') can spoil an otherwise effective piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure conclusions sustain rather than undercut the poem's established tone or moral impression. Re-evaluate final lines to avoid unintended implications that weaken the work's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective use of musicality and ballad elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'power of music' and ballad-singer qualities (e.g., Vincent Bourne's town scenes or ballad-singer in the Seven Dials) are valuable when they suit the poem's subject and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhythm, songlike phrasing, and musical devices where they reinforce mood and theme. The ballad manner can provide force and immediacy when appropriately matched to material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay/paranomasia as a tasteful rhetorical device
rubrics_metrics.description: Paranomasia (punning or near-sound-play) can be a felicitous figure ('That figure is called paranomasia in Greek, I am sometimes happy in it'), but it is a stylistic device rather than the core of good writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ puns and sound-play sparingly and purposefully; they are effective as ornament or lightness but should not substitute for substantive poetic thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction must be 'matter-ful' — substance over mere elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Language should carry real matter; privileging 'fine words' without substantive content is a fault ('What an aching vacuum of matter!' from Lord Thurlow's fine words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words that do work: reveal thought, feeling, or image. Elegant phrasing is good, but not at the cost of emptiness. The best diction is both pleasing and meaningfully freighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and state (MS vs. print) affect reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts read 'raw' and the printed form 'dresses' a work; first impressions differ by medium ('All things read raw to me in MS.; ... I cannot endure my own writings in that state').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that presentation matters: proofreading, arrangement, and final typographic form can alter the work's effect. Allow for editorial and typographic shaping before judging final impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and distinguish works by period for historical/contextual value
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier poems should perhaps be kept distinct as belonging to a particular period ('I have hitherto kept them distinct in my mind, as referring to a particular period of your life').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assembling or editing collected works, consider preserving chronological/contextual groupings so readers can appreciate development and historic interest; avoid conflating distinct creative phases that were meaningfully different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary concessions to critics that diminish originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not sacrifice lines or elements to 'those scoundrels' (malicious critics); giving critics 'an inch' invites more demands and may harm the work ('You say you made the alteration for the "friendly reader;" but the "malicious" will take it to himself').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defend essential features of the work; be cautious about altering art to appease anticipated hostile readings. Artistic choices should be made for aesthetic reasons, not merely to placate reviewers.
